newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Secret Israel-PLO summit fails to seal Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Secret Israel-PLO summit fails to seal Hebron deal.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu and the Palestinians' Yasser Arafat met secretly in the middle of the night on Sunday but failed to break their deadlock on a self-rule deal for Hebron, sources on both sides said.

The sources, who declined to be identified, said U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, trying for months to broker a deal on the West Bank town, took part in the summit at the Erez crossing between Israel and the Palestinian-ruled Gaza Strip.

Ross had been scrambling to arrange a summit between Prime Minister Netanyahu and President Arafat to seal an accord but Israeli, Palestinian and U.S. sources said no agreement was reached during the meeting.
Palestinian sources said the meeting began at 2 a.m. and lasted four hours. They said another summit could take place later on Sunday.

The sources said they discussed coming to terms on the elusive deal to give Palestinians self-rule in 80 percent of the volatile town as well as setting target dates for the Israeli handover of rural parts of the West Bank.
Officials on both sides were tight-lipped about the news or else acted surprised when asked about it.
"I have no comment," Netanyahu's political adviser Dore Gold, told Reuters.
In Gaza, Arafat ignored questions about the meeting, which reporters shouted at him when he entered his office on Sunday.
The Hebron handover has been held up for 10 months because of security issues and other concerns. Some 400 Jews live and study in the heart of the town surrounded by 100,000 Arabs.

Underscoring tensions, witnesses said that as news of the meeting leaked out, unidentified assailants hurled a petrol bomb in front of a building inhabited by Jews in the town. No one was hurt and no damage was caused.

Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat said that despite the snags, a deal would be signed in the West Bank town of Jericho on Monday to station 210 international observers in Hebron once Israeli troops redeploy.
He said the observers would come from Denmark, Italy, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
Under a 1995 interim agreement, international observers are to be deployed in the town to maintain order, protect residents and monitor violations of the agreement.
Some 400 Palestinian policemen are due to deploy in the Palestinian-ruled part of Hebron.
Officials for the two sides, who last week predicted an imminent deal, accused each other of causing a delay.
"Mr Arafat isn't ready to close the deal on the basis of the agreements that have already been made," Gold told Reuters.

Palestinians say the central issue blocking an accord is Israel's refusal to commit to a timetable for three further West Bank pullbacks after Hebron in mostly rural areas, as stipulated in previous peace deals.
"There won't be an agreement unless there will be a commitment on the three phases," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israeli army radio on Sunday. Erekat said other issues also had to be resolved.
Against the backdrop of the Hebron issue, Jewish settlers began removing seven mobile homes from a West Bank hilltop on Sunday under a deal reached with government officials.
Their bid on Friday to set up a new outpost near the settlement of Beit El, north of the Palestinian town of Ramallah, drew sharp PLO condemnation.
The settlers said they had struck a deal with the government under which they would remove the caravans in exchange for a meeting with Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai to discuss expanding Beit El.
